replacement: Not long after their return from Euboea, they made a thirty years’ truce with the Lacedaemonians and their allies, and gave up the posts they held in Peloponnese — Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen, and Achaia. In the sixth year of the truce, war broke out between the Samians and Milesians over Priene. The Milesians had the worse of it and came to Athens to complain loudly against the Samians. Some private persons from Samos itself, who wanted to revolutionize the government, joined them. So the Athenians sailed to Samos with forty ships and set up a democracy. They took fifty boys and as many men from the Samians as hostages and lodged them in Lemnos; then they left a garrison in the island and returned home. But some of the Samians had not stayed in the island and had fled to the continent. They came to an agreement with the most powerful men in the city and made an alliance with Pissuthnes, son of Hystaspes, who was then satrap of Sardis. They collected a force of seven hundred mercenaries and crossed over to Samos by night. First they rose against the commons and secured most of them; next they stole their hostages from Lemnos. After that they revolted, handed over to Pissuthnes the Athenian garrison left with them, together with its commanders, and at once prepared an expedition against Miletus. The Byzantines revolted with them.

replacement: The Athenians heard the news and at once sailed against Samos with sixty ships. Sixteen of these never engaged: some went to Caria to watch for the Phoenician fleet, and others to Chios and Lesbos with orders for reinforcements. But forty-four ships under Pericles and nine colleagues gave battle off the island of Tragia to seventy Samian vessels, twenty of them transports, which were sailing from Miletus. The Athenians won. Later they were reinforced by forty ships from Athens and twenty-five Chian and Lesbian vessels. They landed, and since they were stronger on land they surrounded the city with three walls; it was also blockaded from the sea. Meanwhile word came that the Phoenician fleet was approaching to help the Samians; indeed Stesagoras and others had left the island with five ships to bring it. So Pericles took sixty ships from the blockading squadron and left in haste for Caunus and Caria. In the meantime the Samians made a sudden sally and fell on the camp, which they found unfortified. They destroyed the look-out vessels and engaged and defeated those that were launched to meet them. For fourteen days they were masters of their own seas and brought in and carried out what they pleased. But when Pericles arrived, they were shut up again. Fresh reinforcements then came — forty ships from Athens with Thucydides, Hagnon, and Phormio; twenty with Tlepolemus and Anticles; and thirty vessels from Chios and Lesbos. The Samians made a brief attempt at fighting, but could not hold out. After a siege of nine months they surrendered on conditions: they razed their walls, gave hostages, delivered up their ships, and arranged to pay the expenses of the war by installments. The Byzantines also agreed to be subject as before.
